# Fundamental Group of $\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S^1$

**Claim.** $\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, generated by a meridian loop linking the circle once.

## Proof

Let $S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the standard unit circle in the $xy$-plane (the unknot).

### Step 1 — Relate to $S^3 \setminus S^1$

Compactify $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $S^3 = \mathbb{R}^3 \cup \{\infty\}$. Since $S^1 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, the point $\infty$ is **not** on $S^1$, so $\infty \in S^3 \setminus S^1$ and
$$\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S^1 = (S^3 \setminus S^1)\setminus\{\infty\}.$$

### Step 2 — $S^3 \setminus S^1$ is a solid torus

The unknot $S^1 \subset S^3$ has a closed tubular neighborhood $N \cong S^1 \times D^2$ (a solid torus). The standard genus-1 Heegaard splitting of $S^3$ says $S^3 = N \cup (S^3 \setminus \operatorname{int} N)$, where the complement $S^3 \setminus \operatorname{int} N$ is **also** a solid torus. Since $S^3 \setminus S^1$ deformation retracts onto $S^3 \setminus \operatorname{int} N$ (radially push the punctured tubular neighborhood $N \setminus S^1$ onto $\partial N$), we have
$$S^3 \setminus S^1 \;\simeq\; \text{solid torus} \;\cong\; D^2 \times S^1 \;\simeq\; S^1.$$

### Step 3 — Removing $\infty$; reduction to (solid torus) minus a point

Choose $N$ small enough that $\infty \notin N$ (possible since $\infty$ is far from $S^1$). Then $\infty$ lies in the interior of the complementary solid torus $T := S^3 \setminus \operatorname{int} N$. The deformation retraction of Step 2 carries $\infty$ to an interior point $p$ of $T$, so
$$\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S^1 \;\simeq\; T \setminus \{p\}, \qquad T \cong D^2 \times S^1,\quad p \in \operatorname{int}(D^2)\times S^1.$$

### Step 4 — Homotopy type of $(D^2 \times S^1)\setminus\{p\}$

Write $p = (p_0, \theta_0)$ with $p_0 \in \operatorname{int} D^2$. The space $D^2 \times S^1 \setminus \{(p_0,\theta_0)\}$ deformation retracts onto
$$X := (\partial D^2 \times S^1)\;\cup\;(D^2 \times \{\theta_0\}),$$
i.e. the boundary torus $T^2 = S^1 \times S^1$ together with a meridian disk $D^2 \times \{\theta_0\}$ attached along the meridian circle $\partial D^2 \times \{\theta_0\}$.

(Indeed, every point of $D^2 \times S^1 \setminus \{p\}$ can be pushed radially — within $D^2$-fibres away from $p_0$, and along the $S^1$-factor toward $\theta_0$ when near $p_0$ — onto this union.)

### Step 5 — Compute $\pi_1(X)$

The torus $T^2$ has $\pi_1(T^2) = \langle a, b \mid [a,b]\rangle$, where $a$ is the **meridian** ($\partial D^2 \times \{\mathrm{pt}\}$) and $b$ is the **longitude** ($\{\mathrm{pt}\}\times S^1$). Attaching the disk $D^2 \times \{\theta_0\}$ along the meridian $a$ imposes the relation $a = 1$. By van Kampen,
$$\pi_1(X) = \langle a, b \mid [a,b],\; a=1\rangle \;\cong\; \langle b \rangle \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z}.$$

Geometrically, capping the meridian with a disk turns the torus into $S^2 \vee S^1$ (the capped meridian plus collar forms an $S^2$; the surviving longitude is the $S^1$ summand), so $X \simeq S^2 \vee S^1$ and $\pi_1(X) \cong \pi_1(S^1) * \pi_1(S^2) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.

### Step 6 — Conclusion

Combining Steps 1–5,
$$\pi_1(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S^1) \;\cong\; \pi_1(X) \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z}.$$

The generator is the **meridian**: a small loop encircling the removed circle $S^1$ once, i.e. the boundary of a small disk transverse to $S^1$. Its homotopy class corresponds to the longitude $b$ above; it cannot be null-homotoped because any spanning disk would have to intersect $S^1$ (linking number $1 \neq 0$).

### Consistency check (Alexander duality)

For $K = S^1 \cup \{\infty\} \subset S^3$ (two components, $\tilde H^0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$, $\tilde H^1 \cong \mathbb{Z}$), Alexander duality gives
$$\tilde H_i(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S^1) \cong \tilde H^{2-i}(K),$$
yielding $H_1 \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $H_2 \cong \mathbb{Z}$, all other reduced homology vanishing — consistent with $\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus S^1 \simeq S^2 \vee S^1$, whose $\pi_1 \cong \mathbb{Z}$. $\blacksquare$
